title: The devoted son
hookLine: Sama cares for his blind parents and is shot by a king's arrow (Jataka 540)
tomorrow: The king who saw heaven and hell

cards: Early in the day, a young man kneels at a river to fill a water jar, and deer come down to drink beside him, unafraid. In the Jataka his name is Sama, and the water isn't for him.
Back at the hut are his mother and father, both blind, who depend on him for everything. Somewhere in the trees, a king out hunting has already raised his bow.

teach.b: Sama's parents lived as forest ascetics, and the story says they lost their sight to a snake's venom. From then on, Sama was their eyes and hands: water, fruit, washing, a path kept clear.
The king, Piliyakkha, sees a figure among the deer and shoots to bring him down, so he can ask who he is before he runs. The poison takes hold. Sama falls, and he doesn't ask for revenge.
He asks who shot him and why, without anger. Then his thoughts turn to his parents.
Who will bring them water now? The question undoes the king. He goes to the hut himself, tells the blind parents what he's done, and offers to serve them as their son did.
His parents and a goddess who watched over him speak acts of truth, true words about Sama's goodness, and the poison leaves him. He rises and teaches the king.
Look back over the last few days and the same shape keeps returning: Sivi's eyes, the elephant's tusks, the prince who came back, and now Sama at the river.
Each time, someone with every reason to think of himself thinks first of someone else, and pays a price for it. Tradition pairs Sama with the perfection of kindness, metta.

how: Care for parents is part of everyday Buddhist ethics, and the Sama story is told as a picture of a child's devotion; some families make offerings in the names of parents, living and dead.

o: a hunter king who wandered the forest
a forest hermit who lived with deer
a devoted son who cared for his blind parents

games.q: who's who in Sama's story: tap the pairs.
p: the king who shot the arrow

s: Sama cursed the king who shot him
he asked who shot him and why, without anger, and then thought of his parents.
the king offered to serve the blind parents himself
he went to their hut, told them what he'd done, and offered to be their son.
Sama dies at the end of the story
his parents and a goddess speak acts of truth, the poison leaves him, and he rises.

games.q: you're King Piliyakkha. the young man you shot asks only why, and who will bring his blind parents water. what do you do?
o: ride back to the city and say nothing.
go to the hut and offer to serve the parents.
send servants with water and money.
games.why: the king goes to the hut himself, tells the blind parents what he has done, and offers to be their son.

practice: Bring to mind whoever cared for you when you were small, a parent or anyone older who looked after you, living or gone, easy to love or not. Picture one ordinary thing they did for you that they never mentioned, and rest with it.
If they've died, let this be a moment of remembering them well.

wordCard.voice: Sama. The devoted son who cared for his blind parents and, shot by a king, thought first of them. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali Sama, the son's name; the tale is also called Suvannasama, golden Sama.

carryVoice: Your line: who will bring them water. Even as he fell, he thought of them first. Until tomorrow.
